title: What Causes High Triglycerides but Normal Cholesterol?
summary: Why can triglycerides be high when cholesterol is normal? See the common causes, what can throw off the test, why normal LDL can mislead, and which tests to get next.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**High triglycerides with normal cholesterol usually means your body is making or holding on to too many triglyceride-rich particles, while the cholesterol-rich particles a standard panel focuses on stay in range.** The most common reasons are excess weight, insulin resistance or poorly controlled diabetes, alcohol, and diets high in sugar and refined carbohydrates \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]\[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]. Thyroid disease, kidney or liver disease, certain medicines and inherited traits can also be involved \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].


It is worth taking seriously. High triglycerides are linked with a higher risk of heart disease and stroke, and very high levels raise the risk of acute pancreatitis \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. A “normal” LDL on the same report can also be less reliable than it looks when triglycerides are high \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24240933/) \]\[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32101259/) \]. The useful next steps are confirming the result, checking for a cause, and looking at a marker such as non-HDL cholesterol or ApoB that captures what LDL can miss.


## What does “normal cholesterol” mean on a lipid panel?


A standard lipid panel measures total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and[triglycerides](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/triglycerides) , and reports LDL cholesterol, which is usually calculated from the other three rather than measured directly \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/cholesterol-levels/) \]. “Normal cholesterol” usually means total cholesterol and LDL fall inside the healthy range while triglycerides do not.


For adults age 20 and older, MedlinePlus lists these healthy levels \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/cholesterol-levels/) \]:


Marker Healthy level for adults


Total cholesterol Less than 200 mg/dL


LDL cholesterol Less than 100 mg/dL


Non-HDL Less than 130 mg/dL


HDL cholesterol 60 mg/dL or higher is best; below 40 (men) or 50 (women) is low


Triglycerides Less than 150 mg/dL


Triglycerides of 150 to 199 mg/dL are borderline high, 200 to 499 mg/dL are high, and 500 mg/dL or more are very high \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. Your lab report’s own reference ranges are the ones to read your result against.


The two numbers can split because triglycerides and cholesterol are different fats \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) mainly carries triglycerides, while LDL mainly carries cholesterol \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/cholesterol-levels/) \]. When the liver releases more triglyceride-rich VLDL, triglycerides can climb a long way before total cholesterol or LDL moves out of range. For how the two headline numbers relate, see[total cholesterol vs triglycerides](https://mitohealth.com/compare/total-cholesterol-vs-triglycerides) , and for the particle behind the pattern, our explainer on[VLDL cholesterol](https://mitohealth.com/blog/vldl-cholesterol) .


## Why are triglycerides high when cholesterol is normal?


High triglycerides on their own are common: NHLBI estimates that up to one in four adults have high blood triglycerides, and the condition can develop by itself, alongside other lipid problems, or as part of metabolic syndrome \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. When cholesterol is normal, the usual explanations are the ones that push triglyceride production up more than cholesterol:


- **Excess weight and insulin resistance.** Obesity and poorly controlled diabetes are the most common medical conditions behind raised triglycerides \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Alcohol.** Drinking too much raises triglycerides, and alcohol can push them higher in people who already run high \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]\[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Diet.** Eating a lot of sugar and simple carbohydrates, such as foods made with white flour, raises triglycerides \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]. Diets high in carbohydrate raise triglycerides and lower HDL, and adding fructose raises triglycerides \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Low physical activity** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].
- **Medical conditions.** Thyroid disease, kidney disease and liver disease are all listed causes \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. Underactive thyroid more often raises LDL, with triglycerides sometimes mildly raised, and chronic kidney disease is often associated with mildly raised triglycerides \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Medicines.** Diuretics and some medicines that treat breast cancer and HIV can raise triglycerides \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]. Oral estrogen, corticosteroids and some beta blockers are also listed \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Pregnancy.** Triglycerides can rise up to fourfold in the third trimester \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **Genes and ancestry.** Inherited lipid disorders run in families, and NHLBI notes a higher risk in people of South Asian ancestry living in the United States \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].


Several of these often travel together, so finding one does not rule out another. For the full list of causes at every level and the rare symptoms of very high triglycerides, see[symptoms of high triglycerides](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-triglycerides) .


## Is high triglycerides with normal cholesterol dangerous?


It can be, and how much depends on how high the triglycerides are and what else is going on.


- **Heart and blood vessels.** High triglycerides may affect your arteries and raise the risk of coronary artery disease, heart attack and stroke, and they increase the risk of metabolic syndrome \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]. NHLBI notes that non-fasting levels staying above 175 mg/dL for a long time can raise the risk of heart complications \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].
- **Pancreatitis.** NHLBI links levels above 500 mg/dL with a higher risk of acute pancreatitis, a sudden inflammation of the pancreas \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. The Endocrine Society treats levels above 1,000 mg/dL as a pancreatitis risk, and the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline highlights treatment to prevent pancreatitis especially at 1,000 mg/dL or more \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22962670/) \]\[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41824590/) \]\[[9](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/journal-scans/2026/03/13/15/20/acc-aha-release-new-clinical-guideline-for-managing-dyslipidemia) \].


High triglycerides usually cause no symptoms \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. **Sudden pain in the upper abdomen that may spread to the back, especially with nausea, vomiting, fever or a fast heartbeat, needs medical care right away, because it can signal acute pancreatitis** \[[10](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/pancreatitis/symptoms-causes) \].


The opposite pattern, high LDL with normal triglycerides, carries different meaning and is outside this article.


## Why can a normal LDL be misleading when triglycerides are high?


A normal LDL result is least trustworthy exactly when triglycerides are high, for three reasons.


**1. The LDL number is often an estimate.** If your report says LDL is “calculated,” it was worked out from total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/cholesterol-levels/) \]. The long-used Friedewald formula assumes a fixed ratio between triglycerides and VLDL cholesterol, but the real ratio varies \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24240933/) \]. In a study of more than 1.3 million US lipid profiles, people with triglycerides of 200 to 399 mg/dL whose Friedewald LDL came out below 70 mg/dL had a directly measured LDL that was also below 70 only about 40% of the time \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24240933/) \]. An NIH team reported that calculated LDL is less accurate when triglycerides reach 400 mg/dL or more, and developed a newer equation to reduce that error \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32101259/) \]. Mito’s[Lipid Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/lipid-panel) reports LDL as a calculated value, so this applies to it as well.


**2. LDL leaves out the cholesterol in triglyceride-rich particles.** Two numbers you can work out from any standard panel capture it \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]:


- **Non-HDL cholesterol** is total cholesterol minus HDL. It counts the cholesterol in LDL, in triglyceride-rich remnant particles and in lipoprotein(a) together \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]. See[non-HDL cholesterol](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/non-hdl-cholesterol) and how it compares in[triglycerides vs non-HDL cholesterol](https://mitohealth.com/compare/triglycerides-vs-non-hdl-cholesterol) .
- **Remnant cholesterol** is total cholesterol minus LDL minus HDL \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]. When LDL is itself calculated, this number comes straight from the triglyceride result, so it adds little on its own \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]. In a genetic study of 73,513 people in Copenhagen, remnant cholesterol that was 39 mg/dL higher was associated with an estimated 2.8-fold causal risk of ischemic heart disease, though the authors note the finding needs confirmation \[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23265341/) \].


**3. LDL cholesterol can understate the number of LDL particles.** Each LDL, VLDL and remnant particle carries one ApoB molecule, so[ApoB](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/apolipoprotein-b) counts atherogenic particles rather than the cholesterol inside them \[[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7369156/) \]. Once triglycerides rise above about 133 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L), LDL particles carry less cholesterol on average, and LDL cholesterol underestimates how many there are \[[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7369156/) \]. Earlier observational studies found that risk in people with high triglycerides tracked ApoB rather than triglycerides \[[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7369156/) \]. The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline summary says ApoB may be used to assess remaining risk in people with high triglycerides, type 2 diabetes or cardiovascular disease who have reached their LDL and non-HDL goals, and may be a more accurate risk marker than LDL in those groups \[[8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41824590/) \]\[[9](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/journal-scans/2026/03/13/15/20/acc-aha-release-new-clinical-guideline-for-managing-dyslipidemia) \].


## What can throw off a triglyceride test?


Triglycerides respond to a recent meal more than the other numbers on a lipid panel \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \], so one high result is worth confirming before drawing conclusions.


- **A recent meal.** After usual meals, triglycerides rise by about 26 mg/dL on average at their peak, a change a European consensus statement considers small enough that most lipid tests can be done without fasting \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]. For non-fasting samples, it suggests flagging triglycerides of 175 mg/dL or higher as abnormal, rather than 150 \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \].
- **Alcohol.** Regular heavy drinking raises triglycerides \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \], so drinking habits belong in the conversation about the result.
- **Pregnancy, acute illness and medicines.** Triglycerides rise in late pregnancy, in sepsis and critical illness, and with some medicines \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \].
- **A lab artifact.** Most labs measure triglycerides in a way that reads falsely high in rare people with a very high level of glycerol in their blood \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \].


**When to repeat it fasting.** The Endocrine Society recommends basing a diagnosis of high triglycerides on fasting levels \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22962670/) \], and NHLBI describes the diagnosis as fasting triglycerides that are regularly 150 mg/dL or higher \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. The European consensus suggests a fasting sample may be considered when non-fasting triglycerides are above 440 mg/dL \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \]. MedlinePlus notes you may be asked to fast for 9 to 12 hours \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]. Our[guide to fasting before blood work](https://mitohealth.com/guide/fasting-for-blood-work) covers how to prepare.


## Which tests should you get next?


The next tests answer two questions: is the result real, and what is driving it. The Endocrine Society recommends checking people with high triglycerides for secondary causes \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22962670/) \], and a 2024 consensus statement maps each common cause to a screening test \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]:


Question Tests


Is the result real? A repeat[Lipid Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/lipid-panel) , fasting if the first was not


How many atherogenic particles are there?[ApoB](https://mitohealth.com/products/apolipoprotein-b-apo-b) , or the[Advanced Cholesterol Panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/advanced-cholesterol-panel-lipids-apo-b-lipo-a-and-cholesterol-particle-size) , which adds ApoB, Lp(a) and cholesterol particle size to the standard lipids


Is blood sugar involved?[HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hba1c) and fasting[glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/glucose) \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]


Is the thyroid involved?[TSH](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/thyroid-stimulating-hormone) , with free T4 \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]


Are the kidneys involved? Serum[creatinine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/creatinine) with[eGFR](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/egfrcr) , and[urine albumin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-albumin-creatinine-ratio) \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]


Is the liver involved? Liver enzymes such as[ALT](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/alanine-transaminase) \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]


MedlinePlus and NHLBI both note that an ApoB test may be ordered when triglycerides are borderline high, to help judge how high the cardiovascular risk is \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. NHLBI adds that genetic testing may be needed for people with very high triglycerides or pancreatitis without diabetes or obesity, or with a close relative who has very high triglycerides or pancreatitis \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].


Before ordering anything, check your existing report for non-HDL cholesterol. If it is not printed, subtract HDL from total cholesterol yourself \[[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4929379/) \].


## How are high triglycerides usually brought down?


Lifestyle changes come first. NHLBI and MedlinePlus list eating heart-healthy foods and limiting added sugar, getting regular physical activity, aiming for a healthy weight, managing stress, quitting smoking, getting enough sleep and limiting alcohol \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/triglycerides-test/) \]\[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. For very high levels, NHLBI notes a provider may recommend stopping alcohol altogether \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \].


Correcting a secondary cause, such as poorly controlled diabetes or an underactive thyroid, matters before other triglyceride-lowering steps \[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11439749/) \]. Some people also need prescription medicine, and NHLBI notes that more than one may be needed for very high levels \[[2](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/high-blood-triglycerides) \]. Which one, if any, is a decision to make with a clinician.


For a practical walk-through of the food, activity and alcohol changes, see[how to improve your triglycerides naturally](https://mitohealth.com/improve/how-to-improve-your-triglycerides-naturally) , and for the wider heart-health context,[triglycerides and heart health](https://mitohealth.com/blog/triglycerides-working-adults-heart-health) . A repeat lipid panel after making changes shows whether they are working.

## Frequently asked questions


### What happens if cholesterol is normal but triglycerides are high?


High triglycerides still matter when cholesterol looks normal. They are linked with a higher risk of heart disease and metabolic syndrome, and very high levels raise the risk of acute pancreatitis. A normal calculated LDL is also less reliable when triglycerides are high, so non-HDL cholesterol or ApoB can give a clearer picture of cardiovascular risk.


### How can I lower my triglycerides quickly?


There is no proven quick fix. The usual first steps are the ones NHLBI and MedlinePlus list: cutting added sugar and refined carbohydrates, limiting alcohol, regular physical activity and working toward a healthy weight. Treating a cause such as poorly controlled diabetes also matters. Very high levels may also need prescription medicine.


### What can throw off a triglyceride test?


A recent meal raises triglycerides for a few hours, regular heavy drinking raises them, and pregnancy, acute illness and some medicines can push them up. In rare people, a high level of glycerol in the blood makes triglycerides read falsely high. If a non-fasting result is high, a repeat fasting test usually settles it.


### Why are my triglycerides high when everything else is normal?


Triglycerides and cholesterol are different fats carried mostly by different particles, so one can rise while the other stays in range. The most common reasons are excess weight, insulin resistance or poorly controlled diabetes, alcohol, and diets high in sugar and refined carbohydrates. Thyroid, kidney and liver conditions, some medicines and inherited traits can also be involved.
